questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] caching that stays correct: invalidation, stampedes and staleness bounds (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/06). A multi-store catalog serves about 3,000 product-page reads a second at peak, one viral product alone takes 800 a second, and merchants publish about 200 price edits an hour. Six API replicas each keep an in-process cache in front of a shared one. Product pages are read by URL handle, while the merchant admin writes by product id. One store in ten prices by customer segment. The business accepts that a shopper may see an old price for at most 60 s, but a merchant must see their own edit at once. Write your design before you look: what goes into the key, who invalidates and how a missed invalidation would show up, what the staleness bound is on every replica, how a hot key's expiry and a slow origin are absorbed, and how you would prove that a write is visible on the next read. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The read-side key and tags and the write-side invalidation are built by one shared function from one identifier, so a page cached by handle can never be invalidated by id; and an invalidation that matched zero keys is counted and alerted on, because it fails without an error.
keyPoints.quote: derive read and invalidate keys from ONE function

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every input that changes the response (store, customer segment, locale) is part of the key, and segment-priced responses are never stored in a cache that other shoppers read from.
keyPoints.quote: never cache personalized responses at a shared layer

keyPoints.text: [w3] With six replicas, an invalidation that runs only in the process that took the write leaves five stale copies until their TTL expires, so either the invalidation reaches every replica (a broadcast, or only the shared tier holds the entry) or the honest per-replica bound is the in-process TTL, which must then fit inside 60 s.
keyPoints.quote: A local invalidation is only correct when the cache is local to the only writer.

keyPoints.text: [w2] An entry loaded before an edit cannot overwrite the edit after it: cache writes carry a version, and a write older than the last invalidation for that entity is rejected.
keyPoints.quote: version-stamp entries and reject writes older than the last invalidation

keyPoints.text: [w2] The viral key is protected against synchronized expiry: TTLs are jittered so entries written together do not expire together, and stale-while-revalidate lets readers keep the old value while a single refresh runs.
[w2] The cache cannot degrade silently: refresh failures are logged and counted, every in-process cache has a size bound with eviction, and a collapse in hit rate raises an alert.
keyPoints.quote: log and count refresh failures; set an eviction bound (size/LRU); alert on hit-rate collapse

keyPoints.text: [w1] The staleness bound and its owner are written down per cache: which component invalidates, and the worst case it guarantees.
keyPoints.quote: Name the staleness bound and the invalidation owner.

keyPoints.text: [w1] Proof is a test through the real key builders that writes, then reads and expects the new value, plus a TTL test with an injected clock, because a test that never advances time passes even when entries never expire.
keyPoints.quote: a test with an injected clock shows a miss after

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — launch week. A merchant changes a price at 14:03; at 14:25 shoppers still see the old one, the merchant sees the new one, and any pod restarted since 14:03 is correct, so on-call restarts every pod and closes the ticket. The origin database then has a five-minute outage behind the stale-while-revalidate layer, memory on the API pods climbs all week, and the agent inbox fires a burst of requests after every load-balancer idle timeout. What breaks first, how does each problem show, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Warm processes stale, cold processes and the merchant correct, no error: the read side tagged entries with the handle and the publisher invalidated the product id, so the invalidation matched nothing and still reported success; the invalidation counter staying flat after a publish is the tell.

[w3] Stale for 22 minutes, far past any configured TTL, means the TTL is not being enforced: an in-memory store that drops the TTL argument keeps the entry until restart and grows without bound, so restarting pods hides the bug and the climbing memory is the same bug.
[w2] Even with matching tags, a load that started before the edit can finish after the invalidation and store the old price, which then stays until the next invalidation or expiry.
keyPoints.quote: The invalidation happened, and the stale value survives it anyway.

keyPoints.text: [w3] During the origin outage, readers are served stale values until the stale window ends and then block on loads that fail, and because the background refresh errors were swallowed, no metric shows the outage until users do.

[w2] The inbox burst is not wrong data but cost: an unfiltered invalidate-everything on reconnect refetches every cached query at once, and because missed realtime events arrive only through that refetch, the fix narrows it to the queries that can miss events and jitters it rather than deleting it.
keyPoints.quote: This is a stampede created by over-invalidation, not a cache that lies.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your caching choices against the alternatives the chapter names: a TTL or ISR timer alone versus explicit invalidation, a per-process cache versus a shared one, version stamps versus a delayed second delete, stale-while-revalidate versus a blocking reload, invalidating everything on reconnect versus a narrow invalidation, and bypassing the cache for consistency-sensitive reads. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A timer alone needs no invalidation code and its bound is easy to state, but every edit waits out the full bound; explicit invalidation is fresher but adds a failure that makes no noise, so the timer stays behind it as the ceiling.
keyPoints.quote: The live storefront's staleness bound is therefore the ISR timer, not the tag cache.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A per-process cache is the cheapest read there is but cannot be invalidated from another process, so its TTL is a promise about lag (for an auth cache, how long a revoked key keeps working); a shared tier costs a network hop and buys one place to invalidate.
keyPoints.quote: the maximum revocation lag ('undead key' window)

keyPoints.text: [w2] Version stamps close the load-versus-invalidate race exactly but need a monotonic version per entity carried into every cache write; a second delete after a short delay is cheap to add but only shrinks the window, since a load slower than the delay still lands stale.
keyPoints.quote: delete again after a short delay

keyPoints.text: [w2] Stale-while-revalidate keeps latency flat and rides out a short origin outage, but it is exactly what hides that outage, so its stale window becomes that path's real staleness bound and refresh failures must be counted.
keyPoints.quote: If the origin is down, readers keep getting stale data

keyPoints.text: [w3] Invalidating everything on reconnect is simple and correct but turns every network blip into a request spike; removing it would lose missed events; narrowing it to the queries that can miss events, with jitter, keeps correctness at a fraction of the cost.
keyPoints.quote: narrow the reconnect invalidation to the queries that can miss events

keyPoints.text: [w1] Bypassing the cache for low-reuse, consistency-sensitive reads such as the merchant admin gives the merchant read-your-writes at the price of origin load, and it means the merchant sees the truth while shoppers see the stale copy, so the person most likely to report the bug cannot see it.
keyPoints.quote: That bypass is why the merchant in incident 001 sees the right price while shoppers don't.
